parts.latex:
In a group of 60 students, 38 play basketball, 35 play hockey and 5 do not play either basketball or hockey.

How many students play both basketball and hockey?

solutions.latex:
Students who play at least one sport: $60-5=55$.

Using $n(B\cup H)=n(B)+n(H)-n(B\cap H)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 55 &= 38+35-n(B\cap H)\\ n(B\cap H) &= 73-55\\ &= 18\end{aligned}$$

2309.stem: A survey of 150 people found that 113 people liked swimming, 55 liked surfing and 15 liked neither.

figures.cap: Venn diagram of swim and surf with blank boxes
solution sketch: Venn diagram completed: swim only 80, both 33, surf only 22, neither 15

parts.latex:
Use this information to fill in the blank spaces in the Venn diagram.

\exfigure{292_q14_1}
If 2 people are selected at random, find the probability that both people like swimming only.

solutions.latex:
Total $150$, neither $15$, so $150-15=135$ like swimming or surfing or both.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{both}&=113+55-135=33\\\text{swimming only}&=113-33=80\\\text{surfing only}&=55-33=22\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{292_q14_s1}

Swimming only $80$, both $33$, surfing only $22$, neither $15$.
criteria: Fills in two or three of the four regions correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric was half a mark per box; rewritten top-down. Working for the region values added (source gave only the values). Checked: 80+33+22+15=150.
meta.final: Swimming only 80, both 33, surfing only 22, neither 15

solutions.latex:
Both people are chosen from the $80$ who like swimming only, without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{80}{150}\times\dfrac{79}{149}\\&=\dfrac{632}{2235}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: In a group of 60 students, 24 have subscribed to SFLIX and 38 have subscribed to NETAN. If 12 students have subscribed to both SFLIX and NETAN, what is the probability that a student chosen at random has subscribed to neither SFLIX nor NETAN?

solutions.latex:
Students in SFLIX only: $24-12=12$.

Students in NETAN only: $38-12=26$.

Students in at least one: $12+12+26=50$, so $60-50=10$ are in neither.
$$P(\text{neither})=\dfrac{10}{60}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex:
Chemistry, Physics and Biology are three of the subjects students may decide to study. For a group of 50 students, the following is known:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 students study neither Chemistry nor Physics nor Biology
\item 20 students study Chemistry
\item 25 students study Physics
\item 15 students study Biology
\item 9 students study both Chemistry and Physics
\item 10 students study both Chemistry and Biology
\item 11 students study both Physics and Biology
\end{itemize}

A student is chosen at random. By drawing a Venn diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that the student studies all three subjects.

solutions.latex:
Let $x$ be the number studying all three subjects.

The number studying none is 12, so
$$n(\text{at least one subject})=50-12=38$$
Adding the three subject totals gives $20+25+15=60$, and $60-38=22$.

From the Venn diagram regions:
$$\begin{aligned} (9-x)+(10-x)+(11-x)+2x &= 22 \\ 30-x &= 22 \\ x &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{all three})=\dfrac{8}{50}=\dfrac{4}{25}$$
Alternatively, using
$$P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-\big[P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap C)+P(B\cap C)\big]+P(A\cap B\cap C)$$
we get
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B\cap C) &= \dfrac{38}{50}-\dfrac{20+25+15}{50}+\dfrac{9+10+11}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{25} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct Venn diagram or equation for the overlap, or equivalent merit

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

parts.latex: In a class of 30 girls, 13 are dancers and 23 are gymnasts. If 7 girls do both dance and gymnastics, what is the probability that a girl chosen at random does neither dance nor gymnastics?

solutions.latex:
Use the inclusion-exclusion rule for the number who do at least one activity.
$$\begin{aligned} n(D\cup G)&=n(D)+n(G)-n(D\cap G) \\ &=13+23-7 \\ &=29 \end{aligned}$$
So the number who do neither is $30-29=1$.
$$P(\text{neither})=\dfrac{1}{30}$$
Hence the answer is C.

meta.self_check: Venn: 6 dance only, 16 gym only, 7 both, 1 neither = 30.

5457.stem:
In a class of 25 students, each student is required to study at least one of French or German.

It is known that 16 students study French and 18 students study German.

Find the probability that a randomly selected student studies,

parts.latex: both languages given that they study French.

solutions.latex:
Everyone studies at least one language, so the number studying both is $16+18-25=9$.

The number studying only French is $16-9=7$.

$$P(\text{only French})=\dfrac{7}{25}$$

5931.stem: Information was collected from a group of employees at a company regarding their modes of transport to work. Each employee indicated whether they travel by train, bus or both. The results showed that 60% of the employees travel by train, 50% of the employees travel by bus, and 25% of the employees travel by both bus and train. It was also found that 36 employees travel by exactly one mode of transport mentioned.

parts.latex: Show that total number of employees in the company is $60$.
Two different employees are selected at random from the group. Find the probability that neither travel by bus.

solutions.latex:
Let the total number of employees be $n$.

Employees travelling by exactly one mode are those by train only plus those by bus only. Each of these is the total for that mode minus the $25\%$ who travel by both.
$$\begin{aligned} (60\%-25\%)n+(50\%-25\%)n&=36 \\ 60\%\times n&=36 \\ n&=60 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the total number of employees is } 60$$

meta.format_note: Source line $60\%n+50\%n-25\%n-25\%n=36$ rewritten as the equivalent grouped form.

solutions.latex:
Employees not travelling by bus: $50\%$ of $60=30$.

Choosing two different employees without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither})&=\dfrac{30}{60}\times\dfrac{29}{59} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{29}{59} \\ &=\dfrac{29}{118} \end{aligned}$$
